sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV/REF — high confidence on thresholds; no chimney-specific credential)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence on thresholds; no chimney-specific credential
sections.markdown: Alabama runs **two separate contractor boards, and homeowner chimney repair is the residential one's territory.** The **Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board (HBLB)**, under **Ala. Code Title 34, Chapter 14A**, licenses a **"residential home builder"** — defined in **§ 34-14A-2(16)** (paragraph renumbered by Act 2024-443; earlier code years showed it as (12)) to include one who undertakes the construction "or the repair, improvement, or reimprovement thereof" of a residence "when the cost of the undertaking exceeds ten thousand dollars ($10,000)"; **residential roofers** are covered when the cost **exceeds $2,500** (§ 34-14A-2; the HBLB's Jan 29, 2026 public notice restates both lines: a license is required "when the cost of the job is more than $10,000," roofers "more than $2,500"). So a chimney rebuild, reline, or larger masonry repair over $10,000 requires an HBLB license; a homeowner-facing chimney job **at or under $10,000 needs no state license at all.** License type, per the HBLB's published law-and-rules compilation (Oct 2025): a **limited** license covers work that does not affect structural integrity or involves only one trade; an **unlimited** license is required where work affects structural integrity or involves more than one trade (DOC; rule text not independently re-read). Unlicensed residential home building is a **Class A misdemeanor** (§ 34-14A-14(a)), and the board may levy administrative fines "not to exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000) for each violation" (§ 34-14A-14(c)); the HBLB states that under an emergency declaration the crime "may be enhanced to a felony" under Alabama's aggravated home repair fraud statute (section number not given by the board — do not cite one). The separate **Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors (Ala. Code Title 34, Chapter 8)** applies to projects of "one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) or more" (§ 34-8-1(a), raised from $50,000 by **Act 2024-277, effective Oct 1, 2024** — genconbd.alabama.gov). **Act 2026-396 (effective Oct 1, 2026)** adds General Contractors Board exemptions for residential swimming-pool work and "certain routine or regular maintenance, repair, cleaning, and facility support services" — it changes neither the $100,000 line nor the HBLB's $10,000 residential line. A typical homeowner chimney job is far below $100,000. There is **no statewide "home improvement" registration**; any such layer is **LOCAL** (specific city registration regimes not verified this pass). Public lookup: **hblb.alabama.gov** (residential); **genconbd.alabama.gov** (commercial).

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: The HBLB license is a **business/financial-responsibility credential, not a competence exam for flue work.** It is issued on home-builder law and business qualifications (specific exam, experience, and bond requirements not re-verified this pass) — it says **nothing about whether the licensee can diagnose a cracked liner or a spalling crown.** And the whole regime **switches off at $10,000 and below**, which is exactly where most sweeps and small repairs sit. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) are the only real competence signal — a wider gap than in exam-and-bond states like Maryland (labeled comparison).

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV — high confidence; Alabama is a true caveat-emptor state)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; Alabama is a true caveat-emptor state
sections.markdown: **Alabama is a caveat-emptor ("buyer beware") state for resale homes — no statute mandating a seller-disclosure form was identified.** The **Alabama Real Estate Commission** says so on its own consumer page: "The Alabama Supreme Court has held caveat emptor ("buyer beware") to be the law in Alabama when selling existing homes," and "Neither the seller nor the seller's agents, unless asked, are required to disclose defects, except those which might pose an immediate health or safety risk" (arec.alabama.gov, GOV). The controlling case law: in **Blaylock v. Cary, 709 So. 2d 1128 (Ala. 1997)**, the Alabama Supreme Court restated that for used residential real estate "a seller ordinarily has no duty to disclose to the purchaser any defects in the property," subject to three exceptions — (1) a **fiduciary relationship** between the parties; (2) **material defects affecting health or safety** known to the seller but not known to or readily observable by the buyer; and (3) a **direct inquiry** by the buyer, which must be answered truthfully — citing **Cato v. Lowder Realty Co., 630 So. 2d 378 (Ala. 1993)**. **Teer v. Johnston (Ala. Sept. 30, 2010)** reaffirmed that "Alabama retains the caveat emptor rule with regard to the resale of used residential real estate" (quoting **Massey v. Weeks Realty Co., 511 So. 2d 171 (Ala. 1987)**) and called the health-or-safety exception "narrow." Fraud claims for silence rest on **Ala. Code § 6-5-102**: "Suppression of a material fact which the party is under an obligation to communicate constitutes fraud. The obligation to communicate may arise from the confidential relations of the parties or from the particular circumstances of the case." (Case texts read on Justia/FindLaw; § 6-5-102 on the 2025 Justia code — the official code site is script-only and could not be read.) A cracked flue or CO-leaking chimney could plausibly implicate the health/safety exception, but **absent a direct question the seller may stay silent** — the practical takeaway is that Alabama buyers must get their own inspection and ask chimney questions in writing. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: Two levers. **(1)** The **Alabama Deceptive Trade Practices Act (Ala. Code § 8-19-1 et seq.)**, enforced by the AG's Consumer Interest Division, gives a private action under **§ 8-19-10** for "any actual damages sustained ... or the sum of $100, whichever is greater," and the court may award "up to three times any actual damages," plus costs and a reasonable attorney's fee; a written demand at least 15 days before suit is required, and class actions by consumers are barred. **(2)** A **3-business-day cancel right** lives NOT in the DTPA but in the consumer-credit "Mini-Code": **Ala. Code § 5-19-12** — cancel "until midnight of the third business day following execution"; if the seller never gave the required notice, the buyer may cancel within **one year**. **Scope correction:** § 5-19-1(8) defines a home solicitation sale as "a **consumer credit sale** of goods or services" — so this state right covers **financed** doorstep deals only. A **cash** doorstep chimney sale of $25+ at the home is covered by the **federal FTC Cooling-Off Rule (16 CFR Part 429)** — NATIONAL, not Alabama law. Complaints: **Alabama AG Consumer Interest Division** — online form at alabamaag.gov/consumer-complaint/; unlicensed-builder complaints also go to the HBLB (hblb.alabama.gov).

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV — medium; genuine local patchwork, editions unverified)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.confidenceNote: medium; genuine local patchwork, editions unverified
sections.markdown: Alabama has **no single residential code enforced everywhere today — but that is scheduled to change on January 1, 2027.** **Act 2024-443** rewrote **Ala. Code § 34-14A-12**: the HBLB now has "sole authority to adopt" the **Alabama Residential Building Code** and **Alabama Residential Energy Code**, based on "a published edition of the International Residential Code" and of the IECC; created a Residential Building Code Division and an Advisory Council (§§ 34-14A-41 to -44, -80 to -83); and added **§ 34-14A-12.1**, under which, beginning **January 1, 2027**, residential home builders must construct, renovate, or repair per the "applicable residential building code." The state code "shall not supersede any local residential building code adopted by any county or municipality in effect on January 1, 2027"; local codes adopted after that date must meet the state minimums. Enforcement (permits, inspections) stays **LOCAL**, where a building department exists (HBLB law compilation effective Oct 1, 2025 — DOC). **Which IRC edition the HBLB will adopt is NOT yet confirmed** — the Advisory Council was to recommend a code by Oct 1, 2025, and the HBLB homepage links a pending "proposed rule change regarding the Alabama Residential Building Code" on the Legislative Services Agency's admin-code site (script-only; not readable this pass). Birmingham and Huntsville editions also unverified — **do not cite editions yet**. Where a department exists, chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally **permit work**; routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not. In unincorporated/rural areas there may be **no permit process at all** — the local-variance disclaimer is essential here.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — medium; no state statute located)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: Alabama has **no standalone statewide CO-alarm statute located.** **Correction:** an earlier draft said Alabama landlords must provide CO alarms in rentals with fuel-fired appliances or attached garages; the landlord-obligations section of the Alabama Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (**Ala. Code § 35-9A-204**, 2025) contains **no carbon monoxide or smoke alarm provision**, so that claim has been removed. The hotel statute (**§ 34-15-4**) requires smoke detectors in guest rooms but says nothing about CO. CO requirements reach homes only through **locally adopted IRC editions for new construction** (where a local code exists). From **Jan 1, 2027** the state Alabama Residential Building Code (Act 2024-443, § 5 above) will bind HBLB-licensed residential construction statewide — whether the adopted edition carries the IRC's CO-alarm section (R315) is **not yet confirmed**. No statewide pre-sale or pre-rental CO certificate exists. A permitted chimney job remains the natural moment to add alarms. *(Absence of a dedicated CO statute is itself the finding.)*

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime. **North Alabama and the Appalachian foothills carry the real chimney/wood-heat density; the Gulf Coast belt is milder with lighter hearth use** — regionalize accordingly. Not otherwise a material regulatory section for AL.

sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The national pattern is **storm-chaser home-repair fraud** after severe weather: door-to-door and out-of-town contractors, demands for full up-front payment, and no state license shown for jobs over $10,000. Citable agency material: the **AG and HBLB joint warning of Jan 29, 2021** (Jefferson County tornado) — "Ask if they are licensed. Ask to see the card!" and "NEVER make a full payment or substantial down payment up front" (alabamaag.gov); the **HBLB's Jan 29, 2026 "Warning Against Home Repair Fraud"** (license lines $10,000 / roofers $2,500; felony enhancement under an emergency declaration); and an **HBLB license check in Jefferson and Shelby Counties (news item Nov 3, 2025)** that ended in stop-work orders against four unlicensed builders (hblb.alabama.gov, GOV). None of these mentions chimneys. The door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is a DTPA matter, plus § 5-19-12 cancel rights if financed or the FTC Cooling-Off Rule if cash. **No AL chimney-sweep-specific enforcement action located — pattern language only.**

sections.title: Season calendar
sections.markdown: Warm-temperate; colder in the north Alabama highlands, mild on the Gulf Coast. Burn season ~Nov–Feb (short). Rush: OCT–DEC. Best booking: MAR–AUG.

sections.title: Price seeding (internal)
sections.markdown: Birmingham and Huntsville metros run **near-to-slightly-below national**; rural north Alabama and the Gulf Coast below national. Regionalize downward off the national ranges.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Alabama **BREAKS the license⇄disclosure inverse-correlation verdict — it is weak on BOTH axes at once.** The inverse rule says strong-license states (MD, VA) run weak disclosure and strong-disclosure states (IL) run weak licensing; Alabama has **neither**: the residential license is a financial credential that only bites above $10,000 and tests no flue competence, AND there is **no seller disclosure at all** because Alabama is a genuine caveat-emptor state. So Alabama is a **double-vacuum** — the rare state where this site's two core messages collapse into one: **you cannot rely on a state license (it may not exist for your job) OR on the seller (who owes you nothing) — an independent inspection is the only protection.** The oddball mechanical detail: the one hard state cancel right lives in the consumer-*credit* Mini-Code (§ 5-19-12) and only reaches financed sales — cash doorstep deals fall back on the federal FTC Cooling-Off Rule. This makes AL a strong contrast page against caveat-emptor's opposite (e.g., Illinois's named-chimney disclosure form).
